worst_places.quote: A. N+1 query problem causing 5000+ database queries […] The N+1 problem occurs when the resolver for each user separately queries the database for their comments, resulting in 1 query for users + 50 queries for comments = 51 queries total (or worse with nested resolution).
worst_places.problem: graphql-quiz-21. The key option and its own explanation disagree by two orders of magnitude: the option says 5000+ queries (50 users x 100 comments), the explanation computes 51. The article the reader just read (04-n-plus-one-and-dataloader) uses exactly the 1+N arithmetic, so a reader who understood the article will now believe they got the item right for the wrong reason, or that they misunderstood N+1. Same defect in ru («вызывающая 5000+ запросов к базе данных» vs «= 51 запрос всего»).
worst_places.before: A. N+1 query problem causing 5000+ database queries  /  Explanation: … 1 query for users + 50 queries for comments = 51 queries total (or worse with nested resolution).
worst_places.after: A. N+1 query problem: about 51 database queries instead of 2  /  Explanation: The resolver for `comments` runs once per user. So you get 1 query for the 50 users plus 50 queries for their comments = 51 queries. The 100 comments per user do not multiply the query count — they only make each of those 51 queries return more rows. DataLoader batches the 50 comment queries into 1, giving 2 queries total.

worst_places.quote: Sequential execution of Mutations is common but not required, and both can return complex nested data.
worst_places.problem: graphql-quiz-16. This is factually wrong and contradicts three other places on the site. The GraphQL spec REQUIRES serial execution of top-level mutation fields; article 03 calls it «the spec's most underappreciated fact», and graphql-quiz-1 («Mutations are executed serially (not in parallel)») and graphql-quiz-11 («guaranteed to execute serially») state the opposite. Worse: because of this claim, distractor B («Queries execute in parallel, while Mutations always execute sequentially») is marked wrong even though it is true — the item has two correct answers and punishes the reader for knowing the spec.
worst_places.before: Queries are designed for read-only operations with no side effects, while Mutations are the mechanism for operations that modify data. This distinction helps clients understand intent and allows servers to optimize caching and execution strategies. Sequential execution of Mutations is common but not required, and both can return complex nested data.
worst_places.after: Queries are read-only; Mutations are the mechanism for changing data. Both facts in option B are also true — the spec does require top-level Mutation fields to run one after another — so B is not the *primary* difference in terms of side effects, which is what the question asks. Rewrite the distractor instead: B should read "Queries cannot be nested, while Mutations can" (false). Both operation types can return complex nested data.

The explanation dismisses it while the very next sentence of the same explanation, plus graphql-quiz-15, graphql-quiz-20 and article 06 («Кэширование — где REST действительно выигрывает»), all assert that GraphQL caching is harder. worst_places.before: Option C represents a real tradeoff: … Option A is false (GraphQL caching is simpler with Apollo).
worst_places.after: Option C is the tradeoff the question is after: GraphQL usually posts dynamic bodies to one URL, and HTTP/CDN caches key on the URL, so infrastructure-level caching stops working for free. Option A is also true, but it names a client-side cost, not the HTTP/CDN-level tradeoff — Apollo's normalized cache does solve the client side. Option B overstates GraphQL's speed advantage. Option D is wrong: both styles need the same security work.

worst_places.before: Queries are intended for fetching data without side effects, while mutations are designed for operations that modify data on the server. Use queries for read operations and mutations for create, update, or delete.
worst_places.after: Queries read, mutations write — but the spec adds a behavioural difference that interviewers are actually asking about. Top-level Query fields may run in parallel. Top-level Mutation fields must run one after another, in the order they appear in the request. That ordering exists to stop race conditions when one request changes several things: `deductBalance` fully finishes before `addLoyaltyPoints` starts. Nested fields inside a mutation's *result* follow the Query rule again and may run in parallel.

worst_places.before: This three-phase pipeline explains why "GraphQL is strongly typed" does NOT mean "type errors are impossible at runtime." It means: a MISMATCH BETWEEN THE QUERY AND THE SCHEMA is rejected at the Validate phase, BEFORE any resolvers run — i.e., before touching the database. But errors INSIDE a resolver (e.g., the database is down, or a resolver returns `null` for a field typed `String!`) are EXECUTE-phase errors, and they happen at runtime, just like in any other API.
worst_places.after: "GraphQL is strongly typed" does not mean "no type errors at runtime." The three phases show why. A query that does not match the schema is rejected in the Validate phase. No resolver runs, so the database is never touched. But errors *inside* a resolver are Execute-phase errors. The database may be down. A resolver may return `null` for a field declared `String!`. Both happen at runtime, exactly as in any other API.

patterns: The zone has two completely different authors and the reader pays for the seam. The 14 articles are deep, cross-referenced and technically careful; the 30-question bank and 24-item quiz are template-generated at a fraction of the depth and repeatedly contradict the articles they sit next to. Concretely: article 03 states that top-level mutations MUST run serially, quiz-16 states it is 'common but not required'; article 04 states DataLoader turns N+1 into 2 queries, quiz-7 says 'a single batched query'; article 06 states HTTP caching is where REST wins, quiz-25 calls that statement false. A reader working the topic front to back is told opposite things within one session, and the quiz — the layer they meet last — is the one that is wrong.

Generated content in this zone is padded by duplication instead of depth, and the duplication is mechanical enough to be measured. The question bank is 30 entries covering 15 topics, each asked exactly twice (1&6, 2&7, 3&8, 4&9, 5&10, 11&16, 12&17, 13&18, 14&19, 15&20, 21&26, 22&28, 23&27, 24&29, 25&30). The quiz is 24 items covering 6 concepts (Query vs Mutation x4, N+1 x5, fragments x4, Apollo cache x3, introspection x3, GraphQL vs REST x4, plus a missing id graphql-quiz-22). The duplicate slot is spent restating the first answer, so a bank that looks like 30 questions gives 15 topics at ~50 words each, and the senior tier ends up SHORTER (49 words) than the junior tier (72). The fix is not to lengthen sentences — it is to merge each pair into one answer at article depth and spend the freed slots on the senior material the articles cover but the bank never mentions: null bubbling, serial mutation execution, introspection, __resolveType, cursor/Relay pagination, @deprecated and additive evolution, query aliasing, BFF.

Explanatory prose is routinely put inside code blocks. Across all 14 articles, ```txt is used as a general layout device: whole sections (Rate Limiting, Introspection, Authorization, Federation in article 05; every 'Связь с другими темами' and most 'Типичные follow-up' blocks) are body text in a monospace, non-reflowing block hard-wrapped at ~72 characters. For the target reader — phone, short bursts — this is the single most damaging habit in the zone, because it turns readable paragraphs into horizontally scrolling columns. ```txt should be reserved for the genuine ASCII diagrams (the Federation and BFF boxes), and the rest converted to ordinary markdown paragraphs and lists.

Emphasis is done with CAPITAL LETTERS instead of markdown, at a density that reads as shouting and defeats tooling. en/01 has 8 instances in 431 prose words, en/02 6, and the habit runs through every article ('НЕ ВЫЗЫВАЮТСЯ', 'ВСЮ', 'ONE specification', 'THEIR REAL IMPACT', 'AT THE DATABASE LEVEL'). It is also why the flags script reports ONE, EVERY, INSIDE, THEIR, RESULT, AT as unexpanded abbreviations — false positives caused entirely by the style. Bold or italics carry the same emphasis without the cost.
